newsitem.title: UK: Sterling storms to 55-month peak against the mark.
newsitem.headline: Sterling storms to 55-month peak against the mark.

text.p: Runaway sterling stormed to a 55-month peak above 2.82 marks on Tuesday, boosted by strong demand from U.S. investors enticed by the pound's attractive yield, analysts said.

A mixture of other factors, such as the strength of the dollar against the mark and a tough report by the European Monetary Institute on the need for better budget discipline, also added spice to sterling's rally.

"Sterling sentiment is extremely positive, and it continues to be in demand on the back of expectations that interest rate differentials will remain in favour of the UK," said James McKay, UK economist at Paine Webber.
At 1310 GMT the pound traded at 2.8205 marks, up over two pfennigs from 2.7965/74 in late European trading on Monday and just off its 55-month peak at 2.8231.
The Bank of England trade-weighted index, measuring the pound's performance against a basket of currencies, popped above the 100 level to 101.1 for the first time since mid-September 1992.
The pound has been setting fresh peaks since pushing above its old floor of 2.7780 marks in the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) two weeks ago. Its central rate in the ERM was at 2.95.
The backbone of sterling's rally of more than 20 percent against the mark in the past six month is the yield differentials with other European markets.
Ten-year British government bond yields stood at 186 basis points above their German counterparts on Tuesday, the highest in Europe and well above the traditional high-yielders Italy and Sweden.

An indirect boon for sterling also came from the EMI annual report, which expressed serious concern that many European Union countries have not yet managed to rein in their national deficits enough to launch the single currency as planned in January 1999.
"The EMI's latest annual report has raised concern about the fiscal position in Europe, in general, and in Germany," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
Britain's decision to keep its options open on the single currency has given sterling "safe-haven" status.

The likelihood that the pound will stay outside the single currency at its onset - whether or not there is a change of government at the forthcoming election on May 1 - means any nervousness about EMU increases its attraction, analysts said.
"Sterling is outside the ongoing uncertainty in Europe and has consequently benefited from its safe-haven status," said DKB's Stamenkovic.
Even though many analysts expect the pound to weaken in the second half of the year, they see scope for further gains in the short-term , in particular if March jobs data are stronger than expected.

Unemployment data for March, due at 0830 GMT on Wednesday, are likely to show another drop in the total number of people out of work by about 45,000, average forecasts of analysts polled by Reuters showed. In February, the jobless total was down by 68,000.
The pound also firmed against the dollar but its rally was capped by a strong U.S. currency which hit new 37-month peaks of 1.7350 marks in overnight trade.
Sterling/dollar was trading at $1.6274/84 against $1.6213/23 in late Europe on Monday.
